content: Epilepsy is a prevalent neurological disorder globally, with an age-adjusted prevalence ranging from 4 to 8 per 1000 individuals and an incidence of 44 per 100,000 person-years in developed nations. For individuals newly diagnosed with epilepsy, monotherapy is considered the optimal therapeutic approach. This review is an updated version of the Cochrane Review originally published in 2019. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and tolerability of oral clonazepam as a monotherapy for newly diagnosed epilepsy, comparing it to either a placebo or other anti-seizure medications. The databases searched for this review included the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and MEDLINE (Ovid), covering studies up to September 13, 2021. The CRS Web database encompasses randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs from sources such as PubMed, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). The inclusion criteria for this review were RCTs or quasi-RCTs that compared oral clonazepam monotherapy to either a placebo or an active comparator in individuals of any age with newly diagnosed epilepsy. The diagnosis of epilepsy was based on the clinical definition proposed by the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE). The outcomes assessed included the proportion of participants who were seizure-free at one, three, six, 12, and 24 months after randomization; the proportion of responders (defined as those with at least a 50% reduction in seizure frequency from baseline to the end of treatment); the proportion of participants experiencing treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) during the treatment period or discontinuing treatment due to TEAEs; the proportion of dropouts or withdrawals due to side effects, lack of efficacy, or other reasons; and improvements in quality of life as measured by validated rating scales. Two authors independently screened all titles and abstracts to determine the eligibility of studies identified through the search. Data were extracted independently and cross-checked for accuracy. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed, and the certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE criteria. Two RCTs were included in this review, both of which were also part of the previous version of the review. These trials involved a total of 115 participants. One study compared clonazepam to carbamazepine as monotherapy in individuals with newly diagnosed psychomotor epilepsy, now referred to as mesial temporal lobe epilepsy. The other study, published as an abstract, compared clonazepam to ethosuximide as monotherapy in children with absence seizures. Both studies were judged to have an unclear or high risk of bias in most domains, except for the selective reporting domain, where one study was rated as having a low risk of bias and the other as having a high risk of bias. In the study comparing clonazepam to carbamazepine, no significant differences were observed between the two groups in the proportion of participants who were seizure-free at one month (risk ratio [RR] 1.97, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.99 to 3.94; 30 participants; very low-certainty evidence), three months (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.62 to 2.29; 26 participants; very low-certainty evidence), or six months (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.09 to 2.73; 9 participants; very low-certainty evidence) after randomization. Similarly, no statistical differences were found between clonazepam and carbamazepine in the proportion of participants experiencing TEAEs leading to treatment discontinuation (RR 2.61, 95% CI 0.80 to 8.52; 36 participants; very low-certainty evidence) or in the proportion of dropouts or withdrawals due to side effects, lack of efficacy, or other reasons (RR 1.56, 95% CI 0.61 to 4.02; 36 participants; very low-certainty evidence). This study did not provide data on other prespecified outcomes of interest. The study comparing clonazepam to ethosuximide did not report any data on efficacy outcomes. However, the proportion of dropouts or withdrawals was higher in the clonazepam group compared to the ethosuximide group (RR 3.63, 95% CI 1.12 to 11.74; 79 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No additional outcomes of interest were reported in this study. In conclusion, no new studies have been identified since the previous version of this review. The available evidence from RCTs on the efficacy and tolerability of clonazepam as monotherapy for epilepsy is limited and of very low certainty. In a small trial comparing clonazepam to carbamazepine for mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, no differences in efficacy or tolerability were observed. In a trial involving children with absence seizures, clonazepam was less well tolerated than ethosuximide, but no comparative efficacy data were provided. At present, there is insufficient evidence to support the use of clonazepam as monotherapy for the treatment of epilepsy.
